strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical problem: extending VLA-based navigation to full 360° surround-view perception rather than the single front-facing camera used by prior VLA navigation methods, which is a meaningful architectural contribution with clear real-world motivation (thin obstacles, squeezing through gaps, dynamic obstacle avoidance from any direction).

The teacher-student distillation design that trains three specialized RL experts (reaching, squeezing, avoiding) with privileged depth information and distills them into a single RGB-only VLA policy is a sensible way to combine the strengths of RL (access to privileged sensing, capability specialization) and VLA (generalization, robustness to sim-to-real gap) and is reasonably well described.

The capability-balanced data aggregation strategy (weighted travel time gap-based proportional sampling) is a reasonable and mildly novel technical contribution for online DAgger-style fine-tuning across heterogeneous tasks, and the ablation in Fig. 6 shows a plausible benefit over unbalanced aggregation.

The experimental evaluation includes both simulation (against relevant recent baselines: iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) and a reasonably diverse set of real-world scenarios (narrow corridors, thin obstacles, dynamic pedestrians/wheelchairs, cluttered/transparent objects), and the method shows consistent improvements over baselines in SR/CR/WTT across all tested simulation scenes.

The ablation studies (individual vs mixed-capability training, online iteration progress) provide some insight into why combining multiple experts helps and support the claimed synergistic effect of multi-capability training, which is an interesting and non-trivial empirical finding.

The system achieves a practically relevant inference rate (~7Hz) with a 7B-parameter LLM backbone, which is a solid engineering contribution for real-time deployment of VLA policies on a real quadruped robot.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons appear somewhat unfair: iPlanner, ViPlanner, and NavDP are single-camera/front-view methods evaluated against MM-Nav's 4-camera 360° system, so the large performance gap may be substantially attributable to the sensor configuration difference rather than the proposed multi-expert distillation and balancing method; a controlled comparison (e.g., feeding baselines all four views, or comparing against a single-expert/single-view ablation of MM-Nav itself) would better isolate the source of improvement.

There is no comparison to other VLA-based navigation baselines (e.g., NaVid, Uni-NaVid, X-Nav, COMPASS) that are extensively discussed in related work; the only baselines evaluated quantitatively are classical planning-based (iPlanner, ViPlanner) and a diffusion policy (NavDP), leaving the core claim of VLA superiority over other VLA navigation methods unsubstantiated experimentally.

Real-world evaluation is entirely qualitative (Fig. 1, Fig. 5, prose description) with no quantitative success rate, collision rate, or comparison against baselines in real environments, despite the abstract's emphasis on 'extensive real-world experiments' confirming effectiveness; this weakens the evidentiary support for the sim-to-real transfer claims.

Key design choices lack ablation or justification: e.g., the specific loss weight β=5, the choice α=0.3 for smoothing in the capability-balancing formula, ϵ=0.1, and the reward coefficients for RL experts are stated but not justified or ablated, raising reproducibility and sensitivity concerns.

The claim that the VLA student 'outperforms the RL teachers' is presented as a key novel finding, but this could partly stem from the RL experts being under-tuned/limited by scene-specific overfitting or the shared MLP architecture bottleneck (128-256-512 hidden units) rather than a fundamental synergy effect; alternative explanations (e.g., simply more total training data seen by VLA vs. RL) are not ruled out.

No statistical significance / variance reporting (e.g., std over multiple seeds/runs) is given for the 100-episode evaluations, making it hard to assess whether reported differences (e.g., 47% vs 23% SR in Mixed) are robust or could partly reflect stochastic simulation variance.

The paper does not discuss failure cases or limitations of MM-Nav in depth (e.g., where does 20-32% collision rate in Squeezing/Avoiding scenes come from, what specific failure modes remain), which would be valuable given the safety-critical nature of navigation.

The compute/data cost of training three separate RL experts plus iterative online VLA fine-tuning with a 7B LLM (40+ GPU-hours per initial stage plus multiple 2-hour iterations on 8xH100) is significant, and no discussion of scalability to additional capabilities or environments is provided, raising questions about how this approach would extend beyond the three hand-designed capabilities.

strengths: The multi-view (360°) VLA formulation addresses a real limitation of prior front-view-only navigation policies, and the motivation of combining synthetic expert diversity with VLA generalization is reasonable and well-articulated.

The teacher-student DAgger-style pipeline with capability-balanced data aggregation (based on weighted travel time gaps) is a sensible mechanism to combine multiple specialized RL experts into one generalist policy, and the ablations (Fig. 6, Table II) show measurable benefits from balancing and multi-expert mixing over single-expert or unbalanced baselines.

Real-world qualitative demonstrations (thin rope avoidance, squeezing between objects, transparent obstacles, dynamic pedestrian/wheelchair intrusion) are compelling evidence of sim-to-real transfer and reflect practical engineering effort (fisheye undistortion, 7Hz inference, GO2 deployment).

The paper reports a reasonably complete engineering pipeline, including RL expert training details, reward design, and VLA architecture/tokenization choices for efficiency (7Hz inference with a 7B LLM).
weaknesses: Quantitative real-world evaluation is essentially absent: all numeric comparisons (Table I, Table II, Fig. 4, Fig. 6) are conducted purely in simulation; the real-world section is entirely qualitative (a handful of demo clips/figures) with no success-rate, collision-rate, or trial statistics, undermining the claim of 'extensive real-world experiments' and 'robust real-world deployment'.

Baselines in Table I (iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) are all single front-camera methods, making the comparison potentially unfair/predictable given MM-Nav's inherent 360° camera advantage; no multi-view or surround-view baseline is included to isolate whether gains stem from the multi-expert VLA distillation idea versus simply having more cameras.

The key claim that the student VLA outperforms its RL teachers is only demonstrated in simulation using the WTT metric that itself drives the balancing algorithm, which is somewhat circular; no equivalent demonstration is given on real hardware or against stronger multi-view imitation-learning baselines.

Several design choices (reward coefficients in Eq. 3, α=0.3 in capability balancing, history window k=8, loss-balancing β=5) are stated without ablation or justification, raising reproducibility and overfitting-to-setup concerns.

No statistical reporting (variance across seeds/trials, confidence intervals) is provided despite 100-episode evaluations, making it hard to assess the significance of reported gains, especially for close results such as WTT in the Reaching scene where MM-Nav (31.0s) is actually slightly worse than NavDP (27.3s) despite higher SR/lower CR.

Limited discussion of failure cases for MM-Nav itself, either in simulation or real-world; combined with the lack of quantitative real-world metrics, this raises concerns about selection bias in the qualitative demonstrations.

The three hand-crafted capability environments (reaching/squeezing/avoiding) are somewhat ad hoc and specific to this paper's own simulation design; it is unclear how this taxonomy generalizes or scales to additional navigation capabilities beyond the three chosen.

The novelty of individual components (DAgger-style distillation, multi-expert RL teachers, multi-view extension of a video-based VLA) is incremental relative to already-cited prior works (NavDP, Uni-NaVid, X-Nav, COMPASS), with the main contribution being an engineering combination rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical problem: enabling visual-only (no depth/LiDAR) navigation policies to generalize across diverse challenging capabilities (reaching, squeezing through narrow gaps, avoiding dynamic obstacles) using a single unified model, which is a meaningful step for real-world legged/wheeled robot deployment.

The multi-expert teacher-student distillation design is well motivated: it cleverly sidesteps the difficulty of training a single RL policy across heterogeneous, conflicting reward structures by specializing RL experts per capability and then distilling into one VLA student, with empirical evidence (Table II) that the mixed-distilled VLA outperforms both single-capability RL/VLA models and a jointly-trained RL expert, supporting the claimed synergy.

The capability-balanced data aggregation strategy (using weighted travel time gap to reweight online DAgger-style data collection) is a sensible and interpretable mechanism, and the ablation in Fig. 6 credibly shows it converges faster and more evenly than an unbalanced baseline.

Engineering execution for real-time deployment is solid: the paper reports a concrete inference speed (~7Hz) with a 7B-parameter LLM via a tiered visual tokenization scheme, and demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a real quadruped with four fisheye cameras, including qualitatively compelling and difficult scenarios (thin rope, transparent glass, sudden dynamic obstacles).

Quantitative comparisons against three relevant baselines (iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) across four simulated scenes show consistent and fairly large improvements in SR/CR/WTT, and the paper offers plausible qualitative explanations (FOV limitations of front-facing cameras) for baseline failure modes.
weaknesses: Real-world evaluation is almost entirely qualitative (Fig. 1, Fig. 5, narrative description of four scenes) with no quantitative success rates, collision counts, or comparison to baselines in the real world; this makes it hard to assess the actual robustness and reproducibility of the claimed sim-to-real transfer beyond selected demonstrations.

The three RL experts are described as being trained with different, hand-tuned, capability-specific reward coefficients (α, β, γ, δ) chosen via what appears to be manual tuning; the sensitivity of overall system performance to these choices is not analyzed, raising reproducibility concerns.

Baselines used for the simulation comparison (iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) are all single front-facing-camera methods, which the paper itself notes fundamentally limits their FOV; while this supports the case for the 360° design, it also means the comparison partly restates an architectural advantage (more cameras) rather than isolating the contribution of the VLA/expert-distillation framework itself — an ablation with a multi-view non-VLA baseline (e.g., a multi-camera RL/IL baseline) would better isolate the source of gains.
The paper does not report variance/multiple seeds for the 100-episode evaluations, nor confidence intervals, limiting statistical rigor of the comparison in Table I and Table II.

Details on how goal information is obtained/localized in the real world (e.g., is it given via external tracking, odometry drift effects) are not discussed, which is important for assessing practical deployability of the point-goal formulation.

The related-work discussion of discrete-action VLA baselines (NaVid, Uni-NaVid) is not empirically compared against in either simulation or real-world experiments, despite being highlighted as key related methods; a direct comparison would strengthen the significance claims relative to existing VLA-based navigation approaches.

strengths: Well-motivated multi-expert RL-to-VLA distillation framework that decomposes visual navigation into three complementary, hard-to-collect-in-reality capabilities (reaching, squeezing, avoiding), providing a practical route to obtain diverse, safety-critical training data without risking real-world collisions.

Clean multi-view (360°) VLA architecture with an efficient tokenization/pooling design that achieves 7 Hz inference with a 7B-parameter backbone, a non-trivial engineering contribution given the added camera streams.

Thorough and largely convincing experimental validation: results on the public InternVLA-N1 System-1 benchmark (state-of-the-art SR/SPL), a custom IsaacLab benchmark with capability-specific and mixed scenes, and extensive qualitative real-world deployments across four distinct hard scenarios (thin-wire avoidance, cluttered/transparent corridors, pedestrian avoidance, low-light outdoor).

Sensible and empirically validated capability-balanced data aggregation scheme (weighted-travel-time gap-based sampling) with clear ablations showing it outperforms unbalanced training in convergence speed/stability.

Good diagnostic analyses beyond headline numbers: UMAP visualization of VLM latent states shows that VQA co-training measurably closes the sim-to-real distribution gap, and the single- vs multi-view and expert-combination ablations (Table 3) support the claimed synergistic benefit of multi-capability training.
Detailed appendix (RL formulation, reward decomposition, environment construction, hyperparameters) supports reproducibility of the RL-expert component.
weaknesses: Some comparisons may be unfair to the RL experts: they are evaluated out-of-domain (e.g., on InternVLA-N1 benchmark scenes) where their privileged-depth policies were never trained, which inflates the apparent 'VLA surpasses RL teacher' narrative; a same-domain comparison would better isolate the distillation/synergy effect from simple domain-gap artifacts.

Real-world evaluation is largely qualitative; the only quantitative real-world numbers are a small ablation (20 trials/scenario) on VQA co-training, with no head-to-head real-world comparison against other visual navigation baselines (ViNT, NoMaD, NavDP, etc.) that are discussed in Related Work, limiting the strength of the sim-to-real transfer claim.

The three hand-designed capabilities (reaching/squeezing/avoiding) are a useful but somewhat coarse decomposition of navigation skill space; it is unclear how well this taxonomy scales to more diverse real-world behaviors not captured by these three synthetic scene archetypes, and the 'Mixed' test scene, while helpful, is still simulation-only.

Several heuristic hyperparameters (reward coefficients α, β, γ, δ, regularization ε, smoothing exponent α=0.3 in Eq. 6) are introduced with limited principled justification or sensitivity analysis, raising reproducibility/robustness concerns for the capability-balancing mechanism.

Deployment relies on an off-board RTX 5090 server for inference rather than onboard compute, which somewhat undercuts the practical real-time/robotics-deployment framing despite the reported 7 Hz figure.

Tables report single-run success rates without variance/confidence intervals, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported gains (e.g., +15.9 SR points over the best baseline).

Description of the real-world VQA dataset (source, scale beyond '300k/100k' figures, content diversity) is relatively thin, making it hard to judge exactly what real-world knowledge is being transferred and how reproducible this component is.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: bridging the sim-to-real gap for RGB-only, 360-degree visual navigation in cluttered/dynamic scenes without relying on depth or LiDAR.

The overall system (RL expert generation with privileged depth, distillation into a multi-view VLA student, iterative DAgger-style refinement with a capability-balancing mechanism, and VQA co-training) is clearly described with sufficient architectural and training detail (losses, token budgets, reward formulations, hyperparameters) to aid reproducibility.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies: VQA co-training ablation with a UMAP latent-alignment analysis to support the sim-to-real claim, multi-view vs single-view comparison, capability-balanced vs unbalanced data aggregation, and single-expert vs mixed-expert comparisons that illustrate cross-capability transfer.

Reports a large margin of improvement over prior RGB-D/depth-based baselines (DD-PPO, iPlanner, ViPlanner, LoGoPlanner, InternVLA-N1, NavDP, SIDP) on the public InternVLA-N1 System-1 point-goal benchmark, and the finding that the distilled student can surpass its individual RL teachers is an interesting and non-trivial result.

Includes real-world qualitative deployment across several explicitly hazardous/challenging real scenarios (thin wires, cluttered/glass corridors, pedestrians, low-light outdoor scenes), demonstrating some practical feasibility of the approach on a physical quadruped platform.
weaknesses: Real-world evaluation is limited in scale and rigor: only 20 trials per scenario across 4 hand-picked scenarios, with no comparison against any real-world baseline methods (e.g., NavDP, ViPlanner, iPlanner, or other VLA navigators) deployed on the same robot; the real-world results are essentially a self-ablation (with vs. without VQA) rather than a competitive evaluation, which weakens the central sim-to-real transfer claim.

The custom IsaacLab benchmark (Table 2, reaching/squeezing/avoiding/mixed) is constructed by the same authors specifically to match their three training capabilities, so strong performance there is expected and does not convincingly demonstrate generalization beyond the training distribution; the 'Mixed' scene, while described as out-of-distribution, is still built from the same simulator and obstacle primitives.

Baseline coverage for the method comparison is relatively narrow and skewed toward classical/local planners (iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) and does not include other recent VLA-based navigation systems (e.g., NaVid, Uni-NaVid, NavA3, OmniVLA) that are discussed in related work but not empirically compared, making it hard to judge whether gains stem from the proposed pipeline or simply from using a larger, more capable 7B backbone.

The core technical contribution is largely an engineering combination of known ideas (multi-expert RL distillation, DAgger-style iterative refinement, VQA co-training for domain alignment, multi-view VLA tokenization) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic or theoretical advance; the capability-balancing heuristic (Eq. 5-6) is reasonable but ad hoc, with limited justification for the specific functional form and hyperparameters (epsilon, alpha) beyond empirical tuning.

No discussion of the total computational cost/resources required to reproduce the full pipeline (RL expert training + large-scale VLA fine-tuning + iterative online refinement), nor any statement about code or dataset release, which raises reproducibility concerns given the complexity of the pipeline.

Failure case analysis is largely absent; the paper reports success rates and collision rates but provides little insight into when and why the model fails (e.g., specific failure modes in the avoiding/squeezing capabilities, or cases where VQA co-training does not fully close the sim-to-real gap), which would strengthen the honesty and completeness of the evaluation.

strengths: Well-motivated system that addresses a real gap: RGB-only 360° visual navigation with safe handling of squeezing/dynamic-avoidance behaviors that are hard to collect real-world data for, via distillation from privileged-depth RL experts into a single VLA student.

Strong empirical results: on the public InternVLA-N1 System-1 benchmark, MM-Nav improves SR by roughly +15.9 points (88.1% vs 72.2% best prior) using RGB-only input, and the distilled student is shown to match or exceed its own privileged-depth RL teachers, which is a compelling synergy result.

Thorough ablation suite: multi-view vs single-view, VQA co-training (with an interesting UMAP/latent-alignment analysis showing reduced sim-to-real gap as VQA ratio increases), capability-balanced vs unbalanced data aggregation, and expert-combination strategy (mixed-scene single expert vs three specialized experts) all with clear, interpretable trends.

Practical engineering contribution with efficiency emphasis: a 7B multi-view VLA running at ~7Hz via sliding-window token pooling, which is important for real-time robot deployment and comparable to prior single-view VLA navigation speeds.
Reasonably detailed appendix documenting RL expert environments, reward formulation, and hyperparameters, which aids reproducibility of the simulation/training pipeline.

Diverse real-world qualitative demonstrations (thin-wire avoidance, cluttered/glass corridors, pedestrian avoidance, nighttime outdoor scenes) illustrating zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across genuinely challenging conditions.
weaknesses: Real-world quantitative evaluation is limited: only 20 trials per scenario and no real-world baseline comparisons (e.g., against NavDP, ViPlanner, or single-view ablation) are reported in the real world, so the strength of real-world claims rests mainly on qualitative trajectories and the small-N VQA ablation bar chart.

The custom IsaacLab benchmark (reaching/squeezing/avoiding/mixed) used for the main simulation comparisons in Table 2 is built by the authors themselves and tailored to the three capabilities the method is explicitly trained on, which could bias comparisons against baselines (iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) that were not designed around this exact task distribution.

The overall approach is largely a combination of known techniques (capability-specific privileged RL experts, DAgger-style teacher-student distillation, VQA co-training for domain alignment, multi-view VLA tokenization) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the contribution is more of a well-engineered system than a conceptual advance.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported for SR/SPL/WTT results despite stochastic RL training and multiple iterations, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of reported gains, especially in Table 3's individual-capability comparisons.

Details of the real-world/synthetic VQA data composition (source, size relative to navigation data, potential overlap with deployment environments) are only briefly described, leaving some ambiguity about how much of the sim-to-real improvement is attributable to VQA data volume vs. its specific content.

The pipeline's complexity (three separately trained RL experts, iterative online DAgger with capability-balancing, two-stage VLA training) adds substantial engineering overhead and reproducibility burden; no mention of code/data release, which would be important given the many implementation-specific design choices (reward coefficients, thresholds, etc.).

Real-world deployment and generalization are demonstrated only on a single robot embodiment (Unitree Go2); cross-embodiment transfer is explicitly left to future work, somewhat limiting the generality claims made in the introduction.
